result: A complete serial EM reconstruction of a 3-day-old Platynereis larva was performed, identifying 9162 cells with somas and generating 5.66 million skeleton nodes with 28,717 presynaptic and 27,538 postsynaptic sites. Approximately 15-19% of nodes and synaptic sites could not be assigned to cells with somas and remain as fragments.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide comprehensive quantitative data from the reconstruction with explicit numbers for cells, nodes, and synaptic sites. The acknowledgment of unassigned fragments (C4-C5) demonstrates methodological transparency. The data are internally consistent and represent direct observations from the EM volume.

result: The Platynereis larval nervous system consists of an anterior brain connected to a paired ventral nerve cord (VNC) via circumesophageal connectives, with the trunk organized into five segments. The VNC shows organized neuropil architecture with sensory neurons projecting ipsilaterally in ventro-lateral bundles, interneurons with ipsi- or contralateral projections, and motoneurons being the only class with peripheral projections concentrated dorsally.
evaluation: Claims C6-C12 describe the gross anatomical organization of the nervous system with consistent references to figures. The descriptions are based on direct EM observations and represent standard neuroanatomical characterization. The spatial organization of different neuron classes is clearly documented.

result: Neurons show quantifiable morphological properties with median cable lengths of 97.1 µm (varying by neuron type), median of 8 presynaptic and 6 postsynaptic sites, and strong correlations (r>0.7) between cable length and synapse numbers. Most neurons are unipolar with limited branching, and the ratio of pre- to postsynaptic sites distinguishes neuron classes.
evaluation: Claims C13-C19 provide quantitative morphological data with specific measurements and statistical correlations. The Pearson correlation coefficients >0.7 (C18) support the scaling relationships. The data are internally consistent and represent standard morphometric analyses of reconstructed neurons.

result: Neurons generally lack primary cilia, but sensory neurons are bipolar with 0-5 sensory cilia showing different specializations. Interneurons are unipolar or pseudo-unipolar, ciliomotor neurons have two motor axons, and other motoneurons are unipolar.
evaluation: Claims C20-C24 describe ultrastructural features of different neuron classes with citations to prior work (C21, C23). The descriptions are based on EM observations and are consistent with established neuronal morphology. The characterizations are straightforward and well-supported.

result: The synaptic connectome contains 2675 nodes connected by 14,066 directed edges formed by 26,881 synapses, representing a sparse network (density=0.00197). Source nodes are predominantly sensory neurons, sink nodes are mostly effector cells, and high-degree nodes include ciliomotor neurons and specific motoneurons.
evaluation: Claims C25-C30 provide network-level statistics derived from the reconstruction. The graph density calculation and node classifications are standard network analyses. The identification of high-degree nodes is supported by citations to functional studies (C29-C30), linking structure to function.

result: Community detection using the Leiden algorithm identified functional modules in the connectome including the visual circuit, ciliomotor network, anterior neurosecretory centre, mushroom bodies, and mechanosensory modules. These modules show stronger internal connectivity than between-module connections and correspond to functionally characterized circuits.
evaluation: Claims C31-C37 describe module identification using established algorithms (Leiden, C31) with citations. The functional validation of modules through citations to behavioral studies (C34, C35, C37) strengthens the biological relevance. The approach is methodologically sound for identifying functional subnetworks.

result: 966 neurons were classified into 202 cell types (most represented by only 2 cells), and 3128 non-neuronal cells into 92 types including diverse effector cells. Additional developing structures contain immature neurons with few synapses.
evaluation: Claims C38-C44 provide comprehensive cell-type classification with specific numbers. The predominance of bilaterally symmetric cell types (C39) is consistent with the organism's anatomy. The identification of developing structures (C42-C44) demonstrates thoroughness. The classifications are based on multiple criteria described in the methods.

result: The cell-type-level connectome contains 258 cell types (84 sensory, 82 interneurons, 34 motoneurons, 58 effectors) connected by 2410 edges and 14,640 synapses. Left-right connectivity correlation of 0.91 indicates high stereotypy, and network parameters are similar to C. elegans and C. intestinalis connectomes.
evaluation: Claims C45-C48 describe the grouped connectome with clear statistics. The high left-right correlation (C47) supports bilateral symmetry and reconstruction quality. The comparative analysis (C48) provides evolutionary context, though the comparison is qualitative rather than statistical.

result: Sensory-motor pathway analysis identified 4 sensory-motor neurons, 25 premotor sensory neurons, and a maximum path length of 5 hops from sensors to effectors. 33 sensory neurons lack paths to effectors, with 19 being neurosecretory cells.
evaluation: Claims C49-C53 describe circuit depth analysis with specific counts. The identification of neurosecretory cells without effector connections (C53) is biologically plausible as these cells signal through volume transmission. The analysis is straightforward graph-based path finding.

result: Neurotransmitter/neuropeptide phenotypes were assigned to 53 (26%) neuronal cell types, including 11 cholinergic, 3 serotonergic, 1 dopaminergic, 1 adrenergic, 4 glutamatergic types, and 38 types expressing one of 12 neuropeptides. 516 neurons contain dense core vesicles indicating peptidergic transmission.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57 integrate molecular data with connectome reconstruction. The ultrastructural observation of dense core vesicles (C57) corroborates the neuropeptide assignments. The relatively low percentage of assigned phenotypes (26%, C54) reflects the challenge of integrating molecular and anatomical data, but the assignments made are well-supported by citations and EM observations.

result: The head contains 45 sensory neuron types and 52 interneuron types, with information flowing from sensory clusters through interneurons to ciliomotor, ventral motoneuron, and descending interneuron groups. Recurrent connectivity exists between some interneuron clusters.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 describe head circuit organization with specific cell type counts and connectivity patterns. The identification of recurrent connectivity (C60) is important for understanding circuit function beyond simple feedforward processing. The descriptions are based on direct connectivity analysis.

result: Three pairs of ventral head motoneurons (vMNs: MN1-3) form a postural control module with decussating morphology, innervating contralateral ciliated cells and muscles. Additional motor outputs include MNgland-head neurons innervating exocrine glands and several ciliomotor neurons (MC, Ser-h1, MNant, vMN) directly innervating ciliary bands.
evaluation: Claims C61-C66 describe specific motor circuits with citations to functional studies (C61-C62, C64-C65). The decussating morphology and contralateral innervation pattern (C62) is well-documented anatomically. The suggested link between ciliary activity and glandular secretion (C64) is appropriately presented as inference based on connectivity.

result: Visual integration occurs through shared postsynaptic interneurons (INR) between eye photoreceptors and eyespot PRCR1 cells. Network analysis identified MNant and vMN motoneurons with the highest presynaptic partner numbers, INRGW/INarc1/INW interneurons integrating the most inputs, and hCR neurons with the most postsynaptic cell types.
evaluation: Claims C67-C70 identify key integrative neurons through network analysis. The convergence of different photoreceptor types onto shared interneurons (C67) is anatomically demonstrated. The network centrality measures (C68-C70) are standard graph analyses, with the hCR neurons' broad connectivity (C70) supported by citation to functional studies.

result: The mushroom bodies comprise ventrolateral brain ganglia with sensory neurons (SNMB) and interneurons (INMB) classified into intrinsic (MBintrIN) and output (MBON) types. MBs receive inputs from antennae, palps, and other sensory types, showing cell-type-specific connectivity organized into micro-circuits with left-right symmetry (correlation=0.76).
evaluation: Claims C71-C78 provide detailed MB anatomy and connectivity. The classification into intrinsic and output neurons (C73) follows established MB nomenclature. The left-right correlation of 0.76 (C78) is lower than the whole-connectome value (0.91, C47) but still indicates substantial symmetry. The descriptions are consistent with prior partial reconstructions cited (C72).

result: The Platynereis mushroom body shows multilayer, parallel, feed-forward architecture with minimal recurrent connections and fan-out fan-in organization. This multilayer perceptron architecture may support associative memory formation.
evaluation: Claims C79-C80 describe the MB circuit architecture based on connectivity analysis. However, C81 is explicitly speculative ("may support") and cites comparative work in cephalopods rather than direct functional evidence in Platynereis. The architectural description is supported, but the functional interpretation requires experimental validation. The authors appropriately present this as a hypothesis.

result: Head-trunk connectivity involves 138 descending brain neurons and 75 ascending VNC neurons, with 549 trunk cells receiving head inputs and 288 head cells receiving trunk inputs. Trunk-projecting neurons have either decussating or ipsilaterally descending morphologies projecting to different VNC domains, receiving inputs in the head and forming outputs in the VNC.
evaluation: Claims C82-C86 quantify head-trunk connectivity with specific cell counts and anatomical descriptions. The segregation of decussating vs. descending neurons into different VNC domains (C85) and their input-output compartmentalization (C86) are based on direct anatomical observations with figure support.

result: The larval trunk comprises three chaetigerous segments plus a cryptic segment and pygidium, with ciliary bands marking segment boundaries. Connectivity analysis shows strongest within-segment connections but extensive intersegmental connectivity, with some neurons projecting along the entire body length. Different effector types show segment-specific innervation patterns.
evaluation: Claims C87-C96 describe segmental organization and intersegmental connectivity with citations to developmental studies (C87-C88). The connectivity patterns (C90-C96) are based on direct analysis of the connectome. The identification of neurons with "global reach" (C92) is a key finding enabled by whole-body reconstruction.

result: Segment-specific cell types reveal trunk heteromery: segment 1 contains 10 unique types including ciliomotor neurons, segment 2 has 8 types including giant MNspinning motoneurons innervating spinning glands, segment 3 has 2 types, and the pygidium has 7 types including pigment-motor neurons. These form unique segment-specific circuits.
evaluation: Claims C97-C104 document segment-specific cell types with specific counts and detailed circuit descriptions. The MNspinning-spinGland circuit (C99-C101) is particularly well-characterized anatomically. The pygidial pigment-motor neurons (C103-C104) represent a novel finding. The heteromeric organization is clearly demonstrated.

result: Several neuron types (chaeMech, INsplitPB, INbackcross, MNche, MNhose) occur in all chaetigerous segments, and four cell-type families (CR, PU, PB, INsplit) plus two muscle types occur across 5-6 body regions. This pattern may indicate serial homology suggesting metameric evolutionary origin for all body segments including head and pygidium.
evaluation: Claims C105-C106 document serially repeated cell types across segments with specific examples. The evolutionary interpretation (C107) is appropriately presented as inference ("may indicate") based on the anatomical pattern. The serial homology hypothesis is a reasonable interpretation of the data, though it requires comparative evidence for full support.

result: The mechanosensory girdle is an anatomically distinct system spanning the entire body with a circumoral ring continuing in two VNC tracts. It includes penetrating mechanosensory neurons (CR, PB, PU, interparaPM) with cilia surrounded by microvilli expressing polycystin mechanoreceptors, plus chaeMech chaetal mechanoreceptors.
evaluation: Claims C108-C112 describe a novel anatomical system with clear morphological criteria. The molecular characterization (C111) is supported by citations. The identification of this system as a distinct entity is justified by its anatomical coherence and shared molecular markers. The circumoral organization is particularly notable.

result: ChaeMech neurons are dendritic sensory cells in segments 1-3 with dendrites branching between chaetal sacs, potentially sensing chaetal displacement during crawling or external stimuli. They show similarities to bristle receptors in other annelids and dendritic proprioceptors in Drosophila, projecting to the VNC with mixed input-output compartments and connecting to premotor interneurons and motoneurons.
evaluation: Claims C113-C119 characterize chaeMech neurons anatomically and compare them to similar cells in other species (C115-C116). The functional speculation about proprioception (C114) is appropriately tentative. The comparative descriptions (C115-C117) are based on citations. The connectivity analysis (C118-C119) is directly supported by the connectome data.

result: ChaeMech neurons strongly innervate INsplitCR interneurons, which are also postsynaptic to collar receptors (CR) mediating startle responses. However, chaeMech and CR circuits are only partially overlapping, suggesting chaeMech may provide proprioceptive inhibitory feedback during startle through INsplitCR cells.
evaluation: Claims C120-C126 analyze the convergence and divergence of mechanosensory pathways. The connectivity patterns (C121-C125) are directly observed in the connectome. The functional hypothesis about proprioceptive feedback (C126) is appropriately presented as speculation ("suggests that there may be") based on the circuit architecture and cited functional studies of CR neurons (C122).

result: INsplit interneurons (pseudounipolar morphology) are the main postsynaptic partners of mechanosensory neurons, subdivided into distinct types (INsplitCR, INsplitPB, etc.) occurring across trunk segments and head with cell-type-specific connectivity. They are premotor neurons connecting to motoneurons innervating all effector types, thus mechanosensory neurons provide input to all body effector systems.
evaluation: Claims C127-C135 characterize the INsplit family comprehensively. The cell-type-specific connectivity patterns (C129-C132) are directly observed. The high network centrality (C133) is supported by graph analysis. The conclusion that mechanosensory input reaches all effector systems (C135) logically follows from the connectivity data (C134).
